projects.name: Provide daily school meals and take home rations to children in public primary schools
projects.description:
WFP:
WFP is implementing the Home-Grown School Feeding Programme and providing daily school meals to 77,264 school children from 324 public schools in Montserrado, Margibi, Bong, Nimba, and Maryland Counties. 
WFP had contracted 15 Farmer Cooperatives to aggregate and supply the 324 schools with locally grown rice, beans, red palm oil, and gari.

WFP will deliver 324 institutional energy efficient stoves to the supported schools. 
20 school gardens and 5 school farms will be established focusing on meal diversification, sustainability, and economic activities for the communities. 
324 school administrators will be trained in school feeding management and implementation.
WFP School Connect digital application will be rollout in additional 249 schools to enhance enrollment, attendance, food deliver and consumption tracking.

projects.name: Support implementation of the Accelerated Community Development Programme
projects.description:
In 2024, the Accelerated Community Development Programme (ACDP) delivered transformative impacts across rural Liberia by implementing key initiatives in water, agriculture, and health sectors. These efforts were designed to address critical gaps in basic services while empowering communities economically and socially.

The ACDP completed five solar-powered boreholes and 21 water kiosks in five rural communities across Gbarpolu, Bong, and Rivercess Counties. Four kiosks in Donfah, Bong County, are already operational, providing sustainable and clean drinking water. This initiative has significantly reduced the time and effort residents, particularly women and children, spend fetching water, improving overall quality of life.

The ACDP supported 14 farmers' cooperatives in six counties (Bomi, Bong, Gbarpolu, Lofa, Nimba, and Rivercess) with tractors, improved rice seeds, fertilizers, technical training, and financial assistance. These cooperatives cultivated large-scale rice and cassava crops, some for the first time. By December 2024, 12 cooperatives had harvested a total of 4,742 bags (25kg each) of paddy rice, benefiting 725 cooperative members (435 women, 290 men). These interventions are boosting productivity and transforming the livelihoods of cooperative members through sustainable income generation.

To enhance technical backstopping for rural farmers, the ACDP procured and handed over 16 YAMAHA motorbikes to the Ministry of Agriculture. These motorbikes were distributed to extension officers, enabling them to provide timely supervision, training, and monitoring. This logistical support has resolved longstanding challenges in reaching remote farming communities, ensuring consistent support to farmers.

The ACDP handed over seven ambulances to the Ministry of Health for deployment in rural health facilities across seven counties (Bomi, Lofa, Margibi, Maryland, Nimba, Rivercess, and River Gee). Since their deployment in July 2024, these ambulances have played a vital role in strengthening emergency medical responses, facilitating 340 emergency cases, including safe maternal deliveries. The ambulances have reduced referral times and improved access to critical healthcare services, significantly benefiting underserved rural communities.

projects.name: Provide rural women, smallholder farmers with access to finance around food value chains
projects.description:
Over 40 Savings and Loans Associations are:
Breaking down barriers to finance – The associations are helping the women overcome common barriers, and access to finance has been one such barrier for many of them because there is a lack of limited or no formal financial institutions in their communities.
Empowering women to become changemakers – The women in the associations are investing in CSA and vegetable production because of loans taken from their respective SLAs. They have been able to make a profit. Also, the SLAs are not just about increasing income or serving as a social protection fund, they have also empowered the women to become active players in their various communities.
Promoting solidarity and equality – Being part of such successful community associations has led to inspiring gains in the women’s social status. They are starting their own businesses and are participating in community decision-making processes at the household and community levels. Being able to contribute financially within their families has even put the women on a more equal footing with their spouses.
Contributing to peace building – financial freedom for women from a combination of the SLAs and other businesses is enabling women to support peacebuilding efforts at the community level.

projects.name: Support communities to increase productivity, enhance sustainable livelihoods, resilience capacities, social inclusion, food and nutrition security
projects.description:
13 women-based farming cooperatives are practicing climate-smart and nutrition-sensitive agriculture techniques. This is evidenced by the CSA techniques the women farmers are using in planting and growing rice, cassava, plantains, and maize (corn). The women are also practicing nutrition-sensitive agriculture demonstrated by their growing of different varieties of vegetables.  

WFP - 750 smallholder farmers received different training to enhance sustainable agriculture production and input support which helped them to adopt climate smart agriculture practices to increase production. Vulnerable farmer organizations resilience capacity strengthened through providing them with training, agricultural inputs, and machinery support to increase production and value addition.
Additionally, WFP created market access to smallholders farmer groups through purchase of locally grown food commodities (861.91 MT) at the value of US$1,900,000.00. This helped to boost agriculture production of smallholder farmers including increasing household incomes and improve food access for smallholder famers and families .

In 2025, UN Women is providing a total of 82,000 USD (Activity ID: 2.1.3) to support communities in Liberia to increase productivity, enhance sustainable livelihoods, resilience capacities, social inclusion, financial inclusion, and food and nutrition security. This support aligns with "Activity ID: 2.1.3: Support communities to increase productivity, enhance sustainable livelihoods, resilience capacities, social inclusion, financial inclusion, food and nutrition security, including the provision of agri-equipment, pre & post-harvest management training, etc" and encompasses several key initiatives.

Firstly, efforts to strengthen agricultural productivity and sustainability include Solar Power Agri-Equipment Support for Women Cooperatives, receiving two grants totaling 19,000 USD (14,000 USD from the UN Women HQ small grant and 5,000 USD from UN Women). This aims to enhance agricultural practices through the adoption of sustainable energy solutions. Secondly, promoting financial inclusion is addressed through Financial Inclusion Support for Women Cooperatives, allocated a budget of 20,000 USD from UN Women to improve women's access to formal financial services. A significant component focuses on Empowering Rural and Young Women through Capacity Building, with a budget of 25,000 USD from UN Women. This initiative targets women from UN Women-supported networks (e.g., NRWS, NaPHWoL, AWICBT, LMA, etc.) and will provide training in financial inclusion, green and blue economies, entrepreneurship and trade, care economy awareness and formalization, and digital literacy skills.

Furthermore, leveraging digital platforms and centers is a key strategy, with Scaling Up the Buy from Women Digital Platform and Establishing Digital Centers supported by a 10,000 USD budget from UN Women. This will enhance the digital platform and expand access to digital literacy and support centers. Building climate resilience and leadership is addressed through NDC 3.0 Training for Youth and Gender Climate Working Group, allocated 5,000 USD from UN Women for capacity building in climate action. Finally, Capacity Development on Organizational Development and Leadership Skills with AWICBT will receive 3,000 USD from UN Women to strengthen the organization.

These interconnected initiatives demonstrate UN Women's commitment in 2025 to fostering holistic and sustainable development for women in Liberia, aligning with the broader goals of increased productivity, enhanced livelihoods, and greater resilience.

projects.description:
UNESCO plans to support the government of Liberia through the Ministry of Education, Ministry of Youth and Sports and the Ministry of Labour for strengthening their data and information management system offering capacity building training to the relevant officials as well as developing webpage in the Ministry's website. It is important that the database of these three ministries are comparatively analyzed and reports are produced to ensure access to need-based education and skills for all age-group learners including children, youth and adults. 

To address the gaps in data, UNICEF has provided critical support to the Ministry of Gender, Children, and Social Protection (MOGCSP) in launching the CPIMS+, to enhance the case management of vulnerable children. Currently operational in Montserrado County, the system is already facilitating the management of 204 cases (88 girls and 88 boys), demonstrating its immediate value in addressing the needs of vulnerable children. The implementation of the CPIMS+ system has strengthened the capacity of 43 social workers by providing a standardized and technology-driven approach to case management. To support CPIMS+, UNICEF procured and donated to the MOGCSP 60 tablets, 11 laptops, 5 laptops and 10 printers. UNICEF has also provided internet subscription. UNICEF has also supported the training of the 43 social workers and supervisors on the use of the system

Development of a new gender and climate change action plan (ccGAP) to coincide with Liberia's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0: Two consultancies are funded for this purpose, with $15,000 USD provided by UN Women Regional Office and $5,000 USD by UN Women Liberia (Sweden's contribution).

projects.description:
Over 100 community leaders, traditional leaders, and religious leaders from 36 communities are changing their perception of PLHIV and the association with SGBV. These leaders are increasingly engaged with implementing the SGBV referral pathway for PLHIV through their participation in ensuring that victims can access medical care, police, psychosocial care, safe homes, and the court. 

Almost 1,500 community members (females: 1,287; males: 209) and 1,412 urban and rural market women are wearing masks and engaged in social distancing and frequent handwashing to prevention COVID-19 infection. In addition, beneficiaries and communities are also cleaning and disinfecting their water and sanitation facilities. 

Misinformation about the coronavirus is being dismissed by the women and their communities. They are promoting all precautionary measures, especially hand washing and the wearing of masks as all beneficiaries gained access to over 14,500 locally produced stitch masks. 

Through the delivery of a comprehensive, sequenced ‘package’ of core interventions (e.g., literacy, numeracy, and business skills; access to finance, etc.) to empower beneficiaries economically and socially, some key results included: 

•	325 women and adolescent girls beneficiaries (those living with HIV/AIDS) in Montserrado, Bong, and Grand Bassa Counties are engaged in small businesses for income generation and better livelihood. They are organizing and managing their own businesses. Their market tables are being transformed into profitable businesses. 
•	Basic literacy and numeracy skills are building the confidence of beneficiaries and unleashing their full potential. 
•	325 beneficiaries are also now saving money as bank account holders while others have gained financial independence which has increased their participation in decision-making.
•	Some 26 local women beneficiaries are demonstrating their potential and resourcefulness as business program coaches and mentors for PLHIV. 
•	13 Savings and Loan Associations (SLAs) are providing financial security and independence for beneficiaries. These associations are offering sustainable, relevant solutions by adding value to a traditionally known and trusted model of saving. 
•	The financial independence gained through established SLAs is increasing women and adolescent girls beneficiaries’ participation in overall decision-making.

14,500 stitch masks were produced by 18 women-led tailoring businesses to prevent COVID-19 infection. Over 575 women beneficiaries received funding to resuscitate their respective SLAs impacted by the pandemic. The SLAs are functioning as self-sustaining and self-managed groups. Peace has remained fragile in cross-border areas where these SLAs are contributing to the provision of a neutral platform for people to dialogue.

•	The SLAs are not only helping women and their families to save their money during the pandemic or to access money. They are also helping them earn for increased economic security and better livelihood during and after the pandemic.

projects.description:
UNDP Liberia: 
In 2024, the Programme continued to support government and civil society organizations (CSOs) to prevent and respond to GBV and pre-trial detention in Liberia. In this regard, the Programme continued its partnership with Development Education Leadership Training in Action Human Right Foundation (DELTA-HRF) and the Efficient Research and Development Institute (ERDI) that enhanced their capacity to support and mentor women led CSOs in Bong and Nimba counties to monitor the performance of Courts E and support GBV/SGBV survivors to access justice and needed services in their communities through the referral pathways. The women led CSOs, with support from DELTA-HRF and ERDI, also monitored the criminal justice system (police, courts, and prison) to identify bottlenecks in the processing of cases and to ensure that cases were processed accordingly. They further provided psychosocial support to survivors, supported survivors and witnesses to access the court (transportation), and conducted community awareness on the existence and functions of the Court E. 
The women led CSO networks in Bong and Nimba supported by DELTA-HRF and ERDI conducted community awareness and education activities on GBV and Court E through radio and community engagements/sensitization. Both DELTA-HRF and ERDI developed and aired radio jingles carrying messages on GBV and Court E on several radio stations in their respective counties. As shown in Table 2 below, the Programme, through these awareness and educational activities, reached 12,258 persons (4,390 men and 7,868 women) via community/house to house sensitization activities, as well as an estimated 80,515 persons through radio jingles. The awareness and education activities has increased the awareness and understanding of the communities on the working of Court E in these counties and enable them to provide support to survivors of GBV/SGBV and respect the rule of law.

projects.description:
In 2025, UN Women is providing a total of $57,000 USD (Activity ID: 2.1.2) to support several key initiatives in Liberia aimed at advancing gender equality and women's empowerment. 4.) Assessment of women's unpaid care work: $5,000 USD from UN Women Liberia (Sweden's contribution) will enable a thorough assessment conducted in collaboration with the Ministry of Gender, Children, and Social Protection to understand the scope and impact of unpaid care responsibilities on women's lives.

5.) Documentation of experiences of vulnerable young women and women living with HIV/AIDS: $15,000 USD from UN Women Liberia (Sweden's contribution) will support the documentation of their perspectives on UN Women's economic empowerment efforts.

This comprehensive support from UN Women aims to contribute significantly to gender-responsive policy advocacy and decision-making across various sectors in Liberia.

projects.name: Provide rural women, smallholder farmers with access to finance around food value chains
projects.description:
Over 40 Savings and Loans Associations are:
Breaking down barriers to finance – The associations are helping the women overcome common barriers, and access to finance has been one such barrier for many of them because there is a lack of limited or no formal financial institutions in their communities.
Empowering women to become changemakers – The women in the associations are investing in CSA and vegetable production because of loans taken from their respective SLAs. They have been able to make a profit. Also, the SLAs are not just about increasing income or serving as a social protection fund, they have also empowered the women to become active players in their various communities.
Promoting solidarity and equality – Being part of such successful community associations has led to inspiring gains in the women’s social status. They are starting their own businesses and are participating in community decision-making processes at the household and community levels. Being able to contribute financially within their families has even put the women on a more equal footing with their spouses.
Contributing to peace building – financial freedom for women from a combination of the SLAs and other businesses is enabling women to support peacebuilding efforts at the community level. 

WFP:

projects.name: Empower women and girls in high burden counties including those living with HIV and AIDS with access to information, services, referral pathways, and economic empowerment opportunities
projects.description:
Over 100 community leaders, traditional leaders, and religious leaders from 36 communities are changing their perception of PLHIV and the association with SGBV. These leaders are increasingly engaged with implementing the SGBV referral pathway for PLHIV through their participation in ensuring that victims can access medical care, police, psychosocial care, safe homes, and the court. 

Almost 1,500 community members (females: 1,287; males: 209) and 1,412 urban and rural market women are wearing masks and engaged in social distancing and frequent handwashing to prevention COVID-19 infection. In addition, beneficiaries and communities are also cleaning and disinfecting their water and sanitation facilities. 

Misinformation about the coronavirus is being dismissed by the women and their communities. They are promoting all precautionary measures, especially hand washing and the wearing of masks as all beneficiaries gained access to over 14,500 locally produced stitch masks. 

Through the delivery of a comprehensive, sequenced ‘package’ of core interventions (e.g., literacy, numeracy, and business skills; access to finance, etc.) to empower beneficiaries economically and socially, some key results included: 

•	325 women and adolescent girls beneficiaries (those living with HIV/AIDS) in Montserrado, Bong, and Grand Bassa Counties are engaged in small businesses for income generation and better livelihood. They are organizing and managing their own businesses. Their market tables are being transformed into profitable businesses. 
•	Basic literacy and numeracy skills are building the confidence of beneficiaries and unleashing their full potential. 
•	325 beneficiaries are also now saving money as bank account holders while others have gained financial independence which has increased their participation in decision-making.
•	Some 26 local women beneficiaries are demonstrating their potential and resourcefulness as business program coaches and mentors for PLHIV. 
•	13 Savings and Loan Associations (SLAs) are providing financial security and independence for beneficiaries. These associations are offering sustainable, relevant solutions by adding value to a traditionally known and trusted model of saving. 
•	The financial independence gained through established SLAs is increasing women and adolescent girls beneficiaries’ participation in overall decision-making.   

All these results have been achieved through strategic partnerships with the Liberian Women Empowerment Network (LIWEN), White Rose Alliance (WRA), the Liberia Marketing Association (LMA), Liberia National Rural Women Structure (LNRWS), the Association of Women in Cross Border Trade, Action for Gender Equality (AGE), and the National Peace Hut Women of Liberia (NPOWOL).

14,500 stitch masks were produced by 18 women-led tailoring businesses to prevent COVID-19 infection. The masks were distributed to 1,958 community members (females: 1,614; males: 344) and 1,412 market women during awareness-raising activities. Beneficiaries are wearing masks and practicing social distancing. They are also engaged in handwashing to prevent infection. 

Over 575 women beneficiaries received funding to resuscitate their respective SLAs impacted by the pandemic. The SLAs are functioning as self-sustaining and self-managed groups. They are actively saving together, and members are taking loans out from their savings. Monitoring missions have found that food poverty amongst SLA members fell from 75% to 20% after just one year of saving. 

Some significant results in response to the socio-economic impact have been recorded:

1.	Peace, solidarity, and equality
•	Being part of such a successful community group has led to impressive gains in women’s social status during the crisis. Members are starting their businesses and taking part in household and community decision-making processes.
 
•	SLA members affected by the pandemic have stressed how their respective groups have helped to improve relations between them and surrounding communities. Peace has remained fragile in cross-border areas where these SLAs are contributing to the provision of a neutral platform for people to dialogue. 

2.	Making money work
•	The SLAs are not only helping women and their families to save their money during the pandemic or to access money. They are also helping them earn for increased economic security and better livelihood during and after the pandemic. 

UN Women continues to bring gender equality and human rights perspectives to its programming on HIV/AIDS with vulnerable women and adolescent girls. It works to ensure that no one is left behind and continues to implement and lead strategic interventions that make clear links to factors that are known to propel the epidemic, such as VAWG, denial of legal rights, and women’s inadequate participation in decision-making processes.
 
UN Women’s HIV/AIDS work has helped to increase the voices of women living with HIV, using tactics that promote their leadership and meaningful participation in all decisions and actions to respond to the epidemic. 
 
UN Women has contributed to the following SDGs:
-	SDG 1: End Poverty by investing in economic empowerment interventions (e.g., business development and access to finance for investing in small businesses, etc.) for reducing poverty and HIV vulnerability. This also includes help in keeping PLHIV healthy.
-	SDG 4: Ensure Quality Education by investing in access to adult education through the provision of literacy and numeracy skills classes for women and adolescent girls including the incorporation of HIV/AIDS training modules into UN Women’s literacy and business skills training curriculums. 
-	SDG 5: Achieve Gender Equality by investing in awareness-raising amongst religious, traditional, and community leaders including community members (men, women, boys, and girls), youth groups, and male networks (HeForShe) for social behavior change to address VAW, SGBV, and the acceptance of marginalized groups (e.g., LGBTQIA, PLHIV, and persons living with disability) to transform social norms, attitudes, and behaviors.

projects.name: Establish a case management system to ensure efficient disposal of cases, reduce case backlog and support online court communication
projects.description:
In 2024, the Programme continued to provide support to the Judiciary to maintain and enhance the functionality of the Judicial Case Management Information System, which was established with the support of the Programme in 2021. The Programme provided advisory and technical support including upgrading of the functions and components of the digital case management system to be make more user-friendly. The Programme also paid the cost of hosting the digital system in the cloud and providing internet subscription that maintained the operations of the system during the year.
These supports helped to maintain the operations and functionality of the system, thereby leading to increased efficiency and effectiveness in tracking of cases on the dockets of magisterial courts across Montserrado County. The migration from manual case management to digital case management is a significant transformational change for the Judiciary, making the filing and retrieval of case files much easier and timely, which will subsequently contribute to reducing cases on courts dockets and reducing pre-trial detention in prisons. One of the reasons that had been attributed to docket and prison overcrowding is tracking cases through the system once the case has been indicted by the court.
The ease of collection, recording, organization, and retrieval of case information is significantly contributing to improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the Judiciary as the entity is able to access information and act on cases in real time, thus reducing the time it would normally take to dispense justice.  Lawyers and magistrates at magisterial courts in Montserrado County are now using the system to assist them plan and assign cases. This is expected to lead to reduction of cases on the courts’ dockets and by extension to the reduction of pretrial detainees in prisons. Pre-trial detention significantly contributes to prison overcrowding in Liberia, as more than 60% of the inmate population is pre-trial detainees.

children.description: UNICEF: A review of Education Management Information System (EMIS) 2014 data related to WASH in Liberian schools revealed that a staggering 55 percent of 4,460 schools in Liberia did not have access to a functional water supply system or facility, 43 percent were without basic sanitation facilities, and only 18 percent had a permanent hand-washing facility. It is equally instructive to note that schools with sanitation facilities had, on average, a ratio of 118 boys per latrine and 113 girls per latrine. UNICEF, in partnership with the Ministry of Education and Public Works, has been working in 14 schools to ensure that 3000 students have access to water and sanitation facilities in schools through the rehabilitation and construction of water points and sanitation facilities in schools, the establishment and training of schools' health clubs, and two solar power water system installations in 2 health facilities, with about 45,0000 people benefiting.
